Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Fast-path light check (single Exa search) surfaced multiple authoritative sources (official EEU tariff schedule, World Bank ESMAP 'Falling Short' tariff survey, UNU-WIDER 2026 reform paper, World Bank GNI data) indicating the row was mislabelled as Unknown; moved to full path. Ethiopia has historically had among the world's cheapest electricity tariffs (around USD 0.12/kWh per a 2020 World Bank survey), but a phased 2024-25 cost-recovery reform raised tariffs substantially (first block from ETB 0.27 to ETB 0.76/kWh by October 2025; top block to ETB 5.10/kWh), while retaining subsidies for consumption up to 200 kWh/month. Calculating cost as a percentage of monthly GNI per capita (approximately USD 92, 2024 Atlas method) varies widely with the assumed consumption baseline: under 1% for a 30-50 kWh subsistence tier (code 5) but roughly 2.5-3% for a typical 200 kWh urban household (code 3), reflecting tiered pricing and birr depreciation (approximately 150 ETB/USD, end of 2025). Given this sensitivity to an unspecified consumption baseline and rapid currency/tariff volatility, revised_value_code is set to 4 as an interim mid-range estimate; flagged for human review to confirm the appropriate consumption assumption and final bucket.
revised_comments: Ethiopia's residential electricity tariffs remain heavily subsidised for basic consumption, with the Ethiopian Electric Utility charging ETB 0.76 per kWh for the first block (up to 50 kWh) following the October 2025 tariff revision, a small fraction of typical household income. Tariffs rise steeply for higher consumption bands (up to ETB 5.10/kWh above 500 kWh), reflecting a phased 2024-25 cost-recovery reform that increased rates substantially from historically among the lowest in the world. Depending on assumed household consumption levels, the cost of electricity ranges from well under 1% to around 3% of monthly GNI per capita (approximately USD 92 in 2024), placing affordability in the moderate-to-affordable range.
